prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After reading the full set of ballots I move B013 from second to first place. It is the only candidate that a clear majority of us (six of eight) placed in the top three, and the reasons given are scientific, not merely habitual. The discovery is concrete and checkable: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the motional and light-shift problem, and Ye's strontium clocks turned the idea into fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, confirmed by independent laboratories and by direct intercomparisons. It is exactly the kind of result I care about, because nature answers back. Clocks at this level test time dilation across millimetres, constrain drifts of constants and dark-matter couplings, and make a redefinition of the second realistic. The attribution is the cleanest on our shortlist, with an inventor and a realizer and no large-collaboration problem, so we can discuss the discovery without a fight over names. Maturity is excellent: more than twenty years of reproduction, and the SI redefinition is being prepared.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision timekeeping has already been rewarded repeatedly (Ramsey, the 2005 comb prize to Hall and Hänsch, Wineland's ion-clock work in 2012), so some of us may see this as a further increment on a well-honoured line rather than a new window on nature. Others (Lemonde, Derevianko, the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups, and ion-clock competitors) also made real contributions, so a two-name credit is a simplification. Finally, the discovery tends to be useful rather than existential: it does not answer a big open question, and I, who like big ideas, feel the pull of candidates such as horizon-scale black-hole imaging or moire quantum matter that change how we picture the world.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a textbook case of a new measurement technique moving the precision frontier by orders of magnitude, with timely maturity because the SI second is up for redefinition.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this, and it is why I am moving B013 up. I would add one qualification: the argument for timeliness should rest on independent intercomparisons at the 1e-18 level and on the physics reach (tests of constants, relativistic geodesy), not on the redefinition of the second, which is a metrological decision and not a scientific verdict. I also want to correct my own opening. I wrote that Ye already shared the 2005 prize; that was wrong. Hall and Hänsch received it, and Ye was Hall's collaborator, so Ye is not a prior laureate and there is no obstacle in that respect.

responses.point: Eriksson puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, because experiment overturned theoretical expectation, the continuum flat-band prediction has been quantitatively tested, and many groups have reproduced the phases.
responses.response: I share the enthusiasm and ranked B046 third, so this is a difference of degree. The flat-band prediction is a genuine theory-meets-nature success. My hesitation is that the thing most people find striking, the superconductivity, still has no accepted mechanism, and the experimental credit is distorted by the credited list omitting Yuan Cao and other first discoverers. A prize for the discovery should fix who found what, and here that is more contested than for the clocks. I would keep B046 as a strong candidate for a coming year, or as my first alternative now, but I do not think the maturity case is as settled as you suggest.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube discovery of astrophysical neutrinos first as a detector-driven new observational window, and puts the Higgs experiments second.
responses.response: I respect the 'new window' logic and I ranked IceCube fifth, not low out of indifference. My concern is attribution. The credited trio of Halzen, Karle and Spiering is plausible, but you yourself say you cannot weigh the many senior collaboration figures and the AMANDA and Baikal predecessors, and a prize that cannot name the right people is risky however good the physics. For the Higgs I share your difficulty: of the four names, at most three can be chosen, and Virdee versus Della Negra is arbitrary. Compared with those two, the lattice clock has a decisive advantage in that we can write its citation without choosing among thousands.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ universality class first as a simple, universal mechanism with exact solutions and a clean liquid-crystal experiment, and notes that the credit list is incomplete.
responses.response: I understand the appeal of a simply stated universal mechanism, and I like that the experiment by Takeuchi and Sano confirms the Tracy-Widom statistics. However, you note yourself that the exact-solution contributors are missing, which makes the credited trio an incomplete answer to the question of who established the picture. Parisi's earlier prize also makes a KPZ citation awkward to word. For me the scientific depth is real but the discovery is less well matched to a statement of 'who did it' than the clocks, so I would not put it in front, though I would like to hear whether the exact-solution work could be credited in a shape that fits three names.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the physics that makes superconducting quantum processors possible, noting that the 2025 prize covered the neighbouring foundation.
responses.response: That 2025 overlap is exactly my worry. A prize for circuit QED so soon after macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits risks looking like one story awarded twice, and the credited trio omits Girvin and others from the original Yale work, as you concede. Clocks and circuits are both mature and both strongly tied to measurement, so I do not consider them far apart in merit, but the clock case has the sharper attribution and no recent adjacent prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to credit only Katori and Ye or whether the contributions of Lemonde, Derevianko and the Sr-clock groups at PTB, SYRTE and NIST require a wider citation.
Whether a fourth timekeeping-related prize in a quarter-century is judged as too incremental relative to a new window on nature.
If the committee prefers a second achievement alongside the clocks, only a single additional name would fit within the three-person limit, which would be hard to justify for B016 or B046.
Falcke, Doeleman and Zensus: I still do not know how the committee will weigh a large collaboration, and my own first-ranked B016 stays uncertain on that count.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the shortlisted candidates is among my mentors, collaborators or PhD supervisor (David Gross is not credited here), and my own research (string theory, de Sitter space, dark bubble cosmology) does not overlap with any shortlisted work. My opening first-place choice, the Event Horizon Telescope, concerns a field close to my interest in black holes but involves no personal tie that I know of.
